p.src: It was these words of Magg's that reminded me of religion. Being, of course, a materialist, I had surely never once given religion any serious thought. But at that time, moved as I was by Tock's death, I began to wonder what the religion of the kappa might be. I immediately put this question to Lapp, the student. “Christianity, Buddhism, Mohammedanism, Zoroastrianism, and the like are all practiced here. But the most influential of all is undoubtedly Modernism. It is also called the Religion of Life.” (“Religion of Life” may not be an entirely accurate translation. The original word is Quemoocha. The suffix cha may be said to correspond to the English “ism.” The root form of quemoo, quemal, means not simply “to live,” but rather “to eat, drink, and copulate.”) “Then there must be churches and temples in this country too?” “You must be joking. Why, the great temple of Modernism is the foremost architectural monument in the country. Why not go and have a look?” One warmish, overcast afternoon, Lapp proudly set out with me for this great temple. It was indeed an immense structure, ten times the size of Nikolai Cathedral. What was more, it combined every conceivable architectural style in a single edifice. Standing before the great temple and gazing at its lofty towers and domes, I even felt something uncanny about it. Indeed, they looked like countless tentacles stretching toward the heavens. We stood motionless before the entrance—how tiny we were even beside that entrance alone!—

p.src: and for some time looked up at that extraordinary great temple, which resembled an enormous monster more than a building.

u.src: and for some time looked up at that extraordinary great temple, which resembled an enormous monster more than a building.

p.src: The interior of the great temple was equally vast. A number of worshippers walked among its Corinthian columns. Yet they, like us, looked exceedingly small. Presently we encountered a stooped old kappa. Lapp bowed slightly to him and then addressed him politely. “Elder, I am very glad to find you in good health.” The other kappa bowed in return and replied with equal courtesy. “Why, is that you, Mr. Lapp? You are looking as—” (He broke off for a moment, perhaps because he had only just noticed that Lapp's beak was decaying.) —ah, at any rate, you seem to be keeping well. But what brings you here today...?” “Today I have come as this gentleman's companion. As you probably know, this gentleman—” Lapp then launched into a long and fluent account of me. It also appeared to serve as an excuse for Lapp's seldom visiting the great temple. “And so I wonder if I might ask you to show him around.” The elder smiled with dignified composure, greeted me first, and quietly pointed toward the altar at the front. “Though you ask me to guide you, there is little I can do to help. What we believers worship is the ‘Tree of Life’ upon the altar before you. As you can see, the ‘Tree of Life’ bears fruits of gold and green. The golden ones are called the ‘Fruits of Good,’ and the green ones the ‘Fruits of Evil.’ ...” In the course of this explanation, I had already begun to feel bored. For even the elder's well-meant words sounded to me like an ancient metaphor. Naturally, I pretended to be listening intently.

p.src: But I did not forget, from time to time, to steal a glance around the interior of the great temple.

p.src: Corinthian columns, Gothic vaults, a floor with an Arabian-looking checkerboard pattern, a prayer desk imitating the Secession style—the harmony created by these things possessed a strangely barbaric beauty. What caught my eye above all, however, were the marble busts in the niches on either side. I felt that I somehow recognized those figures. Nor was that so strange. When the stooped kappa had finished explaining the “Tree of Life,” he approached the niche on the right with Lap and me, and began to explain the bust within it. “This is one of our saints—Saint Strindberg, who rebelled against everything. It is said that after enduring terrible suffering, this saint was saved by Swedenborg’s philosophy. But in truth he was not saved. This saint merely believed, as we do, in the Religion of Life. —Or rather, perhaps he had no choice but to believe in it. Read the book this saint left us, entitled Legends. The saint himself confesses that he, too, once attempted suicide.” I grew a little melancholy and turned my eyes to the next niche. The bust in the next niche was of a German with a heavy mustache. “This is Nietzsche, the poet of Zarathustra. That saint sought salvation in the Superman he himself had created. But he too remained unsaved and ended by going mad. Had he not gone mad, perhaps he could never have been numbered among the saints. …” After a brief silence, the elder led us to the third niche. “The third is Tolstoy. This saint practiced greater austerities than anyone else.

p.src: That was because, having originally been an aristocrat, he disliked displaying his suffering to the inquisitive public. This saint strove to believe in a Christ in whom belief was, in fact, impossible. Indeed, he even publicly declared that he believed. But toward the end of his life, he could no longer endure wearing that tragic expression. It is well known that this saint, too, sometimes felt terror at the sight of the beam in his study. Yet since he is numbered among the saints, he naturally did not kill himself.”

p.src: The bust in the fourth niche was of one of our fellow Japanese. When I saw that Japanese face, I could not help feeling a sense of affection and nostalgia. “This is Kunikida Doppo. He was a poet who clearly understood the feelings of a laborer about to be run over and killed. But you surely need no further explanation of him. Now, please look into the fifth niche. —” “Is that not Wagner?” “It is. A revolutionary who was a king’s friend. In his later years, Saint Wagner even said grace before meals. But of course, rather than Christianity, it was the Religion of Life to which he belonged. Judging from Wagner’s surviving letters, there is no telling how many times the sufferings of this world drove the saint to the brink of death.” By then we were already standing before the sixth niche. “This is a friend of Saint Strindberg. He is a French painter who began life in business and who, in place of a wife with many children, married a Tahitian girl of thirteen or fourteen. Through this saint’s thick veins flowed the blood of a sailor. But look at his lips. They still bear traces of arsenic or something of the sort. As for the figure in the seventh niche… You must be tired by now. Please come this way, then.” I was indeed tired, so Lap and I followed the elder along a corridor scented with incense and entered a room. In a corner of that little room, beneath a statue of a black Venus, a cluster of wild grapes had been laid as an offering. Having imagined an austere monastic cell without a single ornament, I found this a little surprising. The elder seemed to discern this feeling from my expression, for before offering us chairs, he explained in a half-apologetic manner. “Please do not forget that our religion is the Religion of Life.

p.src: Our god—after all, the teaching of the Tree of Life is: “Live vigorously.” …Mr. Lap, have you shown this gentleman our scriptures?”

u.src: Our god—after all, the teaching of the Tree of Life is: “Live vigorously.”
…Mr. Lap, have you shown this gentleman our scriptures?”

p.src: “No… To tell the truth, I have hardly read it myself.” Scratching the dish on his head, Lap answered honestly. But the elder continued speaking, still smiling serenely. “Then you cannot be expected to understand. Our god created this world in a single day. (Though called the Tree of Life, there is nothing it cannot accomplish.) And that was not all: he also created a female kappa. The female kappa grew so bored that she longed for a male kappa. Our god took pity on her lament, removed the female kappa’s brain, and created a male kappa from it. Our god bestowed on these two kappas the blessing: ‘Eat, mate, and live vigorously.’ …” The elder’s words reminded me of Tock the poet. Unfortunately, Tock the poet was an atheist like me. Since I was not a kappa, it was only natural that I knew nothing of the Religion of Life. But Tock, born in the land of the kappas, must of course have known the Tree of Life. I pitied Tock for the end he had met after failing to follow this teaching, so I interrupted the elder by beginning to speak of him. “Ah, yes, that poor poet.” After hearing what I had to say, the elder let out a deep sigh. “The only things that determine our fate are faith, circumstances, and chance. (Though you people would probably count heredity as well.) Unfortunately, Mr. Tock possessed no faith.” “Tock must have envied you. No, I envy you too. And young Lap here is still so youthful…” “I too might have been an optimist, if only my beak had been sound.” When we said this to him, the elder let out another deep sigh.

p.src: “The truth is, I too—this is my secret, so please do not tell anyone. —The truth is, I too cannot bring myself to believe in our god. But someday my prayers will—” It was just as the elder reached these words. Suddenly the door flew open, and a large female kappa burst in and hurled herself at the elder. Naturally, we tried to restrain her. But in an instant she had thrown the elder down onto the floor. “You old wretch! You stole drinking money from my purse again today, didn’t you!” About ten minutes later, all but fleeing in earnest, we left the elder and his wife behind and descended the steps at the entrance to the great temple. “With a wife like that, no wonder the elder cannot believe in the Tree of Life.” After we had walked in silence for a while, Lap said this to me. But instead of answering, I involuntarily looked back at the great temple. Against the leaden, overcast sky, the great temple still thrust its countless tall towers and domes outward like so many tentacles. All the while it retained the eerie air of a mirage seen in a desert sky. …
